parole.significato: ring (round piece of metal worn around the finger)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese anel, borrowed from Old Occitan anel, from Latin ānellus (“finger ring”). Doublet of elo, which was inherited. Cognates include Catalan anell, French anneau, Italian anello, Spanish anillo. Sense 2 likely comes from the round form of the anus.
From ave (< Latin avis) + Old Occitan estrutz, from Latin strūthiō, from Ancient Greek στρουθίων (strouthíōn).
Borrowed from Old Occitan aize (“comfort”), from Latin adiacēns. Compare French aise and Italian agio. Doublet of adjacente.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese deleitar, from Old Occitan deleitar, from Latin delectare (“to charm”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese desden, borrowed from Old Occitan desdenh, deverbal from desdenhar, from des- + Latin dignāre. Compare Spanish desdén, French dédain.

From Old Galician-Portuguese freire, fraire, borrowed from Old Occitan fraire, from Latin frater (“brother”), from Proto-Italic *frātēr (“brother”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr (“brother”). Doublet of frade, bróder, and brada.

parole.significato: drawer (open-topped box in a cabinet used for storing)
parole.testo: From Old Occitan gaveda, from Latin gabata. Compare Italian gavetta (“mess tin”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese jamais, from Old Occitan ja mais, from Latin iam magis. Cognate with Galician xamais, Spanish jamás, Occitan jamai, French jamais and Italian giammai.
From Old Galician-Portuguese leu, from Old Occitan leu, from Latin levis. Doublet of leve.

parole.significato: palfrey (small horse popular in the Middle Ages)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese palafré, palafrén (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Old Occitan palafren, from Late Latin paraverēdus (“post horse, spare horse”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese perrexil, borrowed from Old Occitan pe(i)ressil, from Latin petroselinum, from Ancient Greek πετροσέλινον (petrosélinon), from πέτρα (pétra, “stone”) + σέλινον (sélinon, “celery”).

parole.significato: tilde, a diacritic (˜). Used in Portuguese to indicate a nasal vowel.
parole.testo: From Old Occitan tille, from Latin titulus. Doublet of título.
From Old Galician-Portuguese torneyo, from Old Occitan tornei, from Latin tornō (“to turn; to lathe”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese viagem, viagen, viage, from Old Occitan viatge, from Latin viāticum. Compare Spanish viaje.
